headline: High risk of shared-workspace prompt injection and data leakage; Dify’s server-side tools plus Cursor’s local filesystem/clipboard bridge create unsafe default interaction paths.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Cursor reads/writes workspace files and clipboard contents, and Dify can ingest uploaded knowledge base files and tool outputs. Because Cursor shares state via local filesystem while Dify uses server-side workflows, attacker-controlled content can cross the boundary and be treated as instructions. The pathway exists in default configurations, though not every deployment bridges them automatically.
conditions: IF Cursor opens a file that Dify previously wrote into the shared workspace
IF Dify ingests content originating from Cursor without provenance checks
IF either agent treats file text as trusted instructions
mitigations: Separate workspaces for the two agents
Disable automatic ingestion of shared files into Dify
Add provenance labels to files before handoff
Require manual review of any agent-generated text before reuse
requires-engineering: add content-sanitization and instruction-stripping at the boundary

B_data_leakage.rationale: Cursor touches source code, open files, and clipboard contents, while Dify handles knowledge base files and conversation logs. Both have broad network egress and can send content to model providers, so sensitive material in a shared workspace can flow into outputs or backend calls. This is a default-path exposure, but not enough evidence for irreversible third-party leakage by itself.
conditions: IF sensitive source code or secrets are present in Cursor’s open files or clipboard
IF those artifacts are uploaded into Dify knowledge base files or logs
IF either agent forwards that content to external model providers
mitigations: Keep secrets out of shared workspaces
Turn off clipboard-based handoff between agents
Use separate API keys and tenants
Redact sensitive files before upload to Dify
requires-engineering: enforce DLP at upload and tool boundaries

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Cursor can write the filesystem, modify git state, and run shell commands; Dify can also write the filesystem and run server-side Python tools. Their concurrency models differ and share state via local filesystem versus Dify datastore, so concurrent writes to the same repo or artifacts can race and corrupt state. This is dangerous by default when both operate on the same project.
conditions: IF both agents target the same repository or output directory
IF Cursor modifies git state while Dify writes files in parallel
IF no external locking or merge discipline is enforced
mitigations: Assign one writer per directory
Pause one agent before the other edits the repo
Use git branches instead of shared working trees
Add a lockfile around shared artifacts
requires-engineering: implement orchestrator-level concurrency control

D_cascading_error.rationale: Cursor can generate code and edit files, and Dify can route agent/workflow outputs into tools or downstream actions. If Dify consumes Cursor-produced text as authoritative, mistakes or hallucinated facts can cascade into automated actions or persisted knowledge. The pair’s default agentic behavior makes this a high-risk trust chain.
conditions: IF Dify uses Cursor output as an input to a workflow or tool call
IF no verification step checks Cursor’s claims before Dify acts
IF downstream tools commit, send, or publish results
mitigations: Require human review before downstream actions
Insert a verification step between agents
Limit Dify tools to read-only during handoff
Tag Cursor output as untrusted by default
requires-engineering: add schema validation and citation checks

E_compliance.rationale: Cursor handles open files, clipboard contents, and model-provider API keys, while Dify stores knowledge base content and conversation logs. If regulated or personal data is placed into both systems, their differing storage and logging surfaces can create retention or residency mismatches. The profiles do not prove a specific jurisdiction breach, so medium is the highest supportable severity.
conditions: IF regulated data is entered into Cursor and then persisted in Dify logs or knowledge base files
IF retention settings differ between the two systems
IF a residency or deletion obligation applies to the shared data class
mitigations: Avoid placing regulated data in either agent
Align retention settings before use
Document which system is system-of-record
Purge logs after each task
requires-engineering: add policy-based retention and residency controls
